newsitem.title: UK: Emerging Eurobonds need steady government bonds.
newsitem.headline: Emerging Eurobonds need steady government bonds.

text.p: A wave of emerging market Eurobonds is expected to swell in 1997, syndicate managers say.
But the sector could be hurt if key underlying government bond markets lose their shine amid rising yields, thus offering investors better returns at a lower risk.
"The thing that could mess it all up is the U.S. Treasury market," WestMerchant head of syndicate Martin Hatt said.
"If U.S. rates rise substantially, then the amount of money going into emerging markets may well decline," Hatt said.

Either this, or there could be a flood of floating rate note (FRN) issuance. But most emerging market investors are traditional fixed-income buyers and are therefore disinclined to buy FRNs, dealers said.
BEST YEAR SO FAR

A sustained and powerful rally in key government bond markets has ensured a spectacular year for the emerging market sector as yield-hungry investors snapped up paper and new issues traders hailed it as the best year thus far.
Capital DATA Bondware showed volumes of new issues from all emerging market borrowers has almost doubled this year to nearly $83 billion from around $45 billion in 1995.

"It has been by far the most successful year across the board in terms of credit rating improvements, size of issues, duration of issues and distribution of credits," ING Barings emerging market syndicate head Manuel Carrellet said.
Added to this, a burgeoning base of better-informed investors has ensured emerging credits have healthy demand.
The political climate has also provided a favourable backdrop for secondary market stability, as have positive economic fundamentals.
A MORE RESILIENT MARKET
Primary market participants said the market was now resilient enough to cope with minor bumps and bruises.
Carrellet said the market had matured a great deal in the past two years and could hold its own in the face of adversity. "The gains of the emerging market are unquestionable.

"For the market to retract to the pre-1995 perception would take a major shake-out and I don't think that's going to happen as the anchoring of the investor base is stronger today than in previous years," he said.
Next year is expected to be an active year for East European issues.

Following Russia's successful debut jumbo Eurobond launch in November, the way is open for the rest of the region to follow suit. Kazakhstan already has and Moscow and St Petersburg are expected in early 1997.
But some dealers said the investor base for Eastern Europe was not as strong as it was for Latin American paper.
"It does not have the loyal investor base Latin America has. So excessive supply could prove difficult as they do not have the depth of demand from North America," Carellet said.
Meanwhile, Argentina and Mexico will have to roll over debt worth up to $20 billion next year. Brazil, Venezuela and Peru are also expected to tap the market.
Added to this, some Latin American countries are being touted as possible candidates for rating upgrades.
China and its entities were also expected to make a name for themselves in the international bond markets but some said it would more towards the millennium.
